newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich says tax deal close with hard negotiating.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich says tax deal close with hard negotiating.

text.p: Americans could soon have their first federal tax cut in more than a decade if legislators and President Bill Clinton participate in some tough negotiations, House Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Sunday.

"I think it will take about a week to 10 days of very hard negotiations and I think in the end, for the first time in 16 years, the American people will get a federal tax cut," Gingrich said on CBS-TV's "Face The Nation" programme.
Gingrich said he believed the president was committed to reaching an agreement.

Last week, Clinton's proposal moved toward Republican priorities on capital gains and estate tax relief. But Clinton sought more tax relief for college education and to give a $500 child tax credit to more lower-income families.

"The president's people want us to take money from taxpayers and transfer it to people who are paying no federal income tax. We don't think a tax cut bill designed to help people who pay taxes should be turned into a welfare bill," Gingrich said. "We'll have to talk that out."
The White House and Congress have had a long-running dispute over how to calculate the impact of proposed tax cuts on the middle class and the wealthy.
Congressional leaders and the president have agreed to find a bipartisan solution to wipe out the budget deficit by the year 2002. That pact included $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years.
Final negotiations were expected to start this week in which one bill would be carved largely from the three proposals offered by Clinton, the House and Senate.
